Purpose The aim of the study was to investigate the effect of a 6-week, low-dose bovine colostrum (BC) supplementation on exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) and performance decline in soccer players following the Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test (LIST) during a competitive season period. Methods In a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled design, two groups of soccer players were allocated to a 3.2 g/day of whey protein (WP, N = 8) or BC ( N = 10) and performed a pre- and a post-supplementation LIST. Maximum isometric voluntary contraction, squat jump (SQJ), countermovement jump, muscle soreness, blood cell counts, creatine kinase (CK), C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) were monitored for 2, 24, 48, 72 h post-LIST. Results LIST induced transient increases in leukocytes, granulocytes, CK, muscle soreness, CRP, IL-6 and declines in lymphocytes and performance indices. Supplementation resulted in a faster recovery of SQJ, CK and CRP compared to pre-supplementation kinetics (trial × time: p = 0.001, 0.056, 0.014, respectively) and lower incremental area under the curve (iAUC) for IL-6, only in the BC group [pre-: 31.1 (6.78–46.9), post-: 14.0 (−0.16 to 23.5) pg h/ml, p = 0.034]. Direct comparison of the two groups after supplementation demonstrated higher iAUC of SQJ [WP: −195.2 (−229.0 to (−52.5)), BC: −15.8 (−93.2 to 16.8) cm h, p = 0.034], a trend for lower iAUC of CK in the BC group [WP: 18,785 (4651–41,357), BC: 8842 (4807–14,802) U h/L, p = 0.081] and a significant intervention × time interaction for CRP ( p = 0.038) in favor of BC. Conclusions Post-exercise EIMD may be reduced and performance better maintained by a low dose of BC administration following LIST in soccer players. Keywords Bovine colostrum Exercise-induced muscle damage Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test Soccer Inflammation Squat jump LR Health and Beauty Systems issue-copyright-statement © Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2018 Introduction Elite-level soccer games are characterized by high-intensity intermittent physical activity. The repetitive and eccentric nature of soccer movements (accelerations, decelerations, kicking, jumping, and tackling) can cause muscle damage, accompanied by the leakage of muscle enzymes and other functional proteins in the circulation, oxidative stress, inflammation and decline in muscle performance [ 1 , 2 ]. The clinical phenotype of post-match muscle damage can strongly impair the recovery process [ 3 ]. Taking into account the congested schedule of elite soccer players (2 or even 3 matches per week) the recovery period is not optimal for the restoration of pre-match exercise capacity and performance, while it may increase the risk for muscle injuries [ 4 ]. Since the extent of muscle damage can determine the duration of the recovery period, several strategies, aiming to attenuate muscle damage and accelerate the recovery period, are under research. However, the majority is adopting physiotherapeutic and training modalities like stretching, cryotherapy, active recovery, sleeping, massage, electrical stimulation and compression garments [ 5 ], while the nutritional or supplementation interventions are much less studied under real post-soccer match conditions. Interventions including the administration of creatine [ 6 ], antioxidant vitamins [ 7 , 8 ], astaxanthin [ 9 ], beta-alanine [ 10 ], omega-3 fatty acids [ 11 ] are tested for their ability to reduce exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) or to increase exercise performance after a soccer match or a simulation of a soccer match. However, the results so far are inconclusive concerning the ability of supplements to improve the recovery process [ 5 ]. Bovine colostrum (BC) is the first milk produced by the mammary glands of the mother during the final days of pregnancy and the first days postpartum (1–4 days). It is as rich in carbohydrates, proteins, fats and micro-nutrients (minerals, trace elements) as the regular milk, but it additionally contains high amounts of oligosaccharides, growth factors, antimicrobial agents and immunoregulatory compounds [ 12 ]. It is therefore a natural multi-ingredient supplement with potential pleiotropic properties. Previous studies focused, mainly, on its effect on exercise performance, body composition [ 13 ], immune system and its ability to counteract upper respiratory tract infections [ 14 ]. However, the doses of BC in these studies were relatively high (20–60 g/day). So far, the ability of BC to enhance the recovery after a high-intensity soccer match is implied only indirectly through its anabolic properties [ 15 ], its buffering capacity [ 16 ] and its ability to attenuate post-exercise intestinal permeability [ 17 ] and oxidative stress [ 18 ]. In order to shed more light on this issue, aim of the present study was to investigate the effect of a low-dose BC supplementation on EIMD and performance in soccer players, during their competitive season, following the Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test (LIST) which simulates the activity pattern of a real soccer match [ 19 ].

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) and performance decline following acute, high-intensity intermittent exercise, such as the Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test (LIST) in soccer players, and the alleviation/enhancement of recovery in this context.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Bovine colostrum (BC) is a natural multi-ingredient supplement rich in oligosaccharides, growth factors, antimicrobial agents, and immunoregulatory compounds. Its ability to enhance recovery is attributed to pleiotropic properties: anabolic effects promoting skeletal muscle synthesis, buffering capacity, attenuation of post-exercise intestinal permeability, and reduction of oxidative stress. Specific mechanisms include modulating post-exercise kinetics through bioactive nutrients (e.g., lactoferrin, lactoperoxidases, lysozyme, IGF-1/2, peptides, oligosaccharides), restricting decrements of IgG2 and salivary IgA, preventing neutrophils degranulation, increasing resting levels of essential and branched-chain amino acids, and antioxidant actions (lowering lipid hydroperoxides, increasing superoxide dismutase and total antioxidant capacity, attenuating xanthine oxidase). It also protects epithelial integrity and attenuates gut permeability by reducing temperature-induced apoptosis and inducing cytoprotective heat-shock proteins. Its mild anti-inflammatory properties further contribute to attenuating muscle damage markers like CK and IL-6.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study utilized a low-dose (3.2 g/day) bovine colostrum (BC) supplementation for 6 weeks, which is considerably lower than the 20–60 g/day often used in previous studies. This low dose was compared against an equal dose of whey protein (WP). The findings indicate that this low-dose BC was effective, with benefits observed while also noting that even a 20-fold higher dose (60 g/day) in other studies did not alter IGF-I/IGFBP-3 or elicit positive doping tests, suggesting the current low dose is safe and close to typical company recommendations (800 mg/day). Pre-supplementation responses to the LIST protocol were similar between WP and BC groups.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: Bovine colostrum supplementation specifically demonstrated significant benefits over whey protein and pre-supplementation conditions, including faster recovery of Squat Jump (SQJ) performance, lower incremental area under the curve (iAUC) for Interleukin-6 (IL-6), a significant intervention × time interaction for C-reactive protein (CRP), and a trend for lower iAUC of Creatine Kinase (CK). BC attenuated post-exercise increments of CRP, CK, and IL-6, and improved SQJ decrements, but did not significantly affect perceived muscle soreness (PMS), overall leukocyte counts, Maximum Isometric Voluntary Contraction (MIVC), or Countermovement Jump (CMJ) kinetics. In contrast, whey protein supplementation showed a limited effect, primarily reducing perceived muscle soreness in knee flexors. The effects of BC were specific to changes in post-exercise plasticity rather than pre-exercise baseline indices, and SQJ performance was found to be more susceptible to BC's effects than CMJ.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Professional and semi-professional soccer players, accustomed to regular eccentric training, participating in competitive seasons and full training schedules (specifically, players from the Greek National league, third and fourth division), as well as healthy adults or athletes engaging in strenuous physical activity and seeking to manage exercise recovery.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Low-dose bovine colostrum (BC) supplementation offers a protective benefit against exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) and promotes faster recovery of muscle performance and inflammatory markers after high-intensity intermittent exercise (simulated soccer matches). It aids in maintaining performance, alleviates EIMD symptoms (e.g., attenuating post-exercise increments of CRP, CK, IL-6), and provides protection against exercise-induced oxidative stress and gut permeability. This can lead to an enhanced recovery process, which is crucial for athletes with congested schedules.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: The intervention is classified as providing a protective benefit and acting as a recovery enhancer, mitigating risks associated with EIMD and performance decline. The low-dose scheme used is considered safe and unlikely to result in a positive doping test. No adverse risks were discussed in the study.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The study utilized a comprehensive panel of established and responsive biomarkers including hematological (WBC, granulocytes, lymphocytes), biochemical (Creatine Kinase, C-reactive protein, Interleukin-6), and performance (Maximum Isometric Voluntary Contraction, Squat Jump, Countermovement Jump) markers, alongside perceived muscle pain (VAS) to assess exercise-induced changes and intervention effects. The Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test (LIST) protocol is well-established for inducing Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage (EIMD) responses comparable to real soccer matches, and the observed responses were consistent. The study controlled for inter-individual variability by comparing pre- and post-supplementation responses within the same volunteers, although the magnitude of CK increase was noted to be lower due to the accustomed nature of the soccer players. SQJ performance was found to be more susceptible to the intervention than CMJ, highlighting differential biomarker sensitivity. The multifactorial nature of EIMD is acknowledged, and while the biomarkers demonstrated utility, the study's limitations include a low number of participants, lack of soccer-specific movements (e.g., tackling, shooting), a limited range of functional tests, and the use of only one BC dose, warranting further validation.
recommended_alternatives: Further mechanistic studies on bovine colostrum's actions on post-exercise recovery
Larger supplementation studies to confirm bovine colostrum's ability to improve recovery after soccer games
